content_voiceover: This page reviews three exam items on AML and MPAL. Question fourteen tests APL treatment, and the wrong statement claims high risk APL, meaning white count over ten times ten to the ninth per liter, should be induced with ATRA and arsenic trioxide alone. High risk APL actually needs an anthracycline added to ATRA, since ATRA-ATO alone is validated mainly for low to intermediate risk disease. Question fifteen tests FLT3 inhibitor pharmacology, and the wrong statement swaps type one and type two inhibitors. Type one inhibitors, like midostaurin, gilteritinib, and crenolanib, block both FLT3 ITD and TKD mutations, while type two inhibitors, like sorafenib and quizartinib, only block FLT3 ITD. Question thirty one covers mixed phenotype acute leukemia. The correct statements are that T myeloid MPAL shares a gene expression profile with early T-cell precursor ALL, and B myeloid MPAL frequently carries ZNF384 fusions. High CD19 expression alone doesn't diagnose B lineage, and MPAL is generally treated with ALL-based, not AML-based, chemotherapy.
keypoints: High risk APL needs anthracycline plus ATRA, not ATRA-ATO alone
Type one FLT3 inhibitors block both ITD and TKD; type two block ITD only
T myeloid MPAL resembles early T-cell precursor ALL by gene expression
B myeloid MPAL often carries ZNF384 fusions
MPAL is generally treated with ALL-based chemotherapy
keypoint_voiceover: Three quick contrasts to lock in. High risk APL needs an anthracycline added to ATRA, ATRA plus arsenic alone is for low risk disease. Type one FLT3 inhibitors like midostaurin and gilteritinib hit both ITD and TKD mutations, type two inhibitors like sorafenib only hit ITD. And for mixed phenotype acute leukemia, T myeloid cases resemble early T-cell precursor ALL genetically, B myeloid cases often carry ZNF384 fusions, and treatment generally follows ALL-based protocols.
